(Tl;dr - we should, IMO, change EM in Lean to one implementation just using ordinary distributions)

I wanted to make a public thread on electromagnetism. I don't think the way it is currently formalized in Physlib is the best way we could do this. Instead of explaining why, I thought it would be nice to motivate what I think is the correct way to formalize electromagnetism.

The real implementation choice in electromagnetism is what sort of mathematical object you let the electric fields, the magnetic field, and the electromagnetic potential be. You could let them be smooth functions, just continuous functions, just square-integrable functions, just integrable functions, etc. To make electromagnetism as useful as possible in Physlib, the choice that we have to make is the one which is as broad as possible. We can then restrict to specific cases as we need them.

To work out what that choice is, it's worth considering what the minimal criterion is in electromagnetism to have a physical theory. Let us use the electric field as an indicator. It is unphysical to demand that we can measure the electric field at every point in space. This is because no measurement device can ever measure a precise point. What we can assume measuring devices can do is measure the electric field in some compact region of space described by some smooth compact profile function η:Space→R\eta : \mathrm{Space} \to \mathbb{R}η:Space→R, often called a test function. Let us call the space of all such functions CCC. So we can say that the electric field EEE takes such compact profile functions and outputs a vector in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 (corresponding to the average of the electric field weighted by the profile function). Thus we have at least a map E:C→R3E : C \to \mathbb{R}^3E:C→R3, based solely on physical assumptions.

What more can we say about E:C→R3E : C \to \mathbb{R}^3E:C→R3 on physical grounds? Well, by considering physically how we expect profiles combine, and how we expect the outputs of profiles close to one another to be related, one can argue that, not only should EEE be linear but it should also be continuous (with some suitable topology on CCC). I won't extend this full argument here.

Such objects have a name: Distributions. Thus on physical grounds, we should be formalising electromagnetism with distributions. But what about the smooth functions, continuous functions etc? Well each of these can be considered as a distribution with some additional regularity property on them. So we lose nothing by working with distributions and then assuming the required regularity property on distributions when needed (e.g. to write down a Lagrangian).

So the idea here is to have 1 copy of EM based on (ordinary) distributions, and then when necessary restrict to special cases of these distributions. (And have sufficient constructors so people only wanting to deal with 'smooth functions' never have to know what a distribution is).

This is to be compared with our approach to EM now in which we have two copies: One for smooth functions and one for tempered distributions. It does not cover any regularity in between.
If people roughly agree with this, maybe the first step is to write a good API-map for this.

Am happy with what you've said above. Though the lean part is still something that I'm trying to wrap my head around, will read through the distribution API in mathlib. It would be to also add a soft view of trying to connect the QED part of the standard model formalization to the distributional framework

I was just yesterday teaching my EM class (second year undergrads) and commenting on how all these point charges and surface charge densities require distributions to bridge the mathematical and physical sense-making. Response was mostly blank stares... But, yeah, I agree with distributions as the basis, and it's a shame we don't teach that to our physicists here in North America :-)

My perspective on this is that tempered distributions forced everything to be global, but a lot of physical phenomenon is described locally, hence I was having a lot of trouble figuring out what formalised EM statements should look like. My understanding on the rigorous formulation is limited, but I agree this is the right move, we just need to be careful about about the refactor because we would be basically overhauling a significant part of the library (looking at this positively it's probably a good opportunity for us to clean up as well)
also this part of mathlib is still under active development; things may change so we should be somewhat cautious
The basic definitions and API for distributions seem pretty solid to me. The API might expand (or perhaps more conveniences may be found), but I personally am not as worried.

My perspective on this is that tempered distributions forced everything to be global, but a lot of physical phenomenon is described locally,

Yes, I think this is the right observation here - tempered distributions where adding unnecessary global conditions on the EM fields. Ordinary distributions do not add such conditions.

Maybe the best way to do the refactor is to leave the functional case as it is right now, and slowly update the distributional case. Then we can eventually remove the functional case.

I should also add, is that one thing I don't know how to fit into my epistemic (or physical led) argument above is the justification that the topology on the set of test functions should match that in Mathlib.

Joseph Tooby-Smith said:

I should also add, is that one thing I don't know how to fit into my epistemic (or physical led) argument above is the justification that the topology on the set of test functions should match that in Mathlib.

Does this need to be resolved before an initial design, to start could the topology of mathlib be a modelling assumption?
No, one could just take it as an assumption. But it would be nice to have a physical reason behind it :).
Okay, I definitely agree that we need a nice physical reason behind, this argument might be more clear as we move towards ordinary distribution?

As a first step would it make sense (I think like mentioned above) to change some of the tempered distribution to ordinary distribution?

For eg if we consider potential to field strength to maxwell equations, I'm wondering is it better to make a parallel ordinary distribution and show the current tempered distribution maps compatibly? Or directly update the tempered distribution
It may make sense to rename the current Distributions file to TemperedDistributions, and then create a new file for ordinary distributions
